briefing.opening: Good morning/afternoon/evening. Welcome. We will now begin the climate briefing for November 10, 2026.

sections.title: 🔴 Deepening Climate Crisis: Domestic and International Impacts and Warnings
sections.content: Recently, the severity of climate change has become increasingly evident both domestically and internationally. 92.2% of Gyeonggi Province residents perceive climate change as directly impacting their lives and health [5, 9, 12], and domestic impacts are materializing, such as Chunyang-myeon implementing preventive education in preparation for the increased risk of large-scale forest fires due to climate change [1]. Particularly in the agricultural sector, damage to pears due to cracking in the Pyeongtaek and Anseong regions has been noted, and there are international reports of farmers struggling due to the Super El Niño phenomenon [23, 115]. The international community warns that climate change efforts could be deemed a 'complete failure' [106], and criticisms continue regarding insufficient global climate action [127], with COP31 opening amidst warnings that 2026 will be one of the hottest years on record [138, 145]. The UN Secretary-General has warned that reliance on oil is detrimental to both the climate and the economy [126], and concerns have also been raised that the climate crisis could push an additional 141 million women into extreme poverty [117, 123].

sections.title: 🌱 Domestic and International Efforts and Technological Innovation Towards Carbon Neutrality
sections.content: Even amidst the climate crisis, various domestic and international efforts and technological innovations towards carbon neutrality are continuing. KIST is responding to calls for expanded research into climate change response technologies by establishing a forest climate change testbed that replicates future heatwaves [2, 11, 13]. Various domestic local governments and institutions are conducting carbon neutrality education [25, 28, 29, 45, 51], and international activities are also vibrant, with Yeosu City making an all-out effort to host COP33 and discussing carbon neutrality and industrial transition at COP31 in Türkiye [6, 20, 43]. Furthermore, Sinopec is practicing ESG management by initiating the creation of a 'carbon-neutral forest' in areas affected by the Yeongdeok forest fire [24, 32, 38, 40], and industry-academia cooperation is also strengthening, with Kyung Hee University and Korea Western Power expanding collaboration on energy transition and carbon-neutral technologies [30, 39, 41, 44, 49]. Internationally, nature-based solutions such as the swan sanctuary wetland restoration project are being pursued [104, 143], and a report suggesting that technology can help achieve carbon neutrality before 2060 is also a positive sign [142].

sections.title: 🇰🇷 Renewable Energy Expansion and Challenges
sections.content: Domestic renewable energy transition is showing progress in various sectors. Discarded water sources such as leaked groundwater, sewage, wastewater, and industrial water have been recognized as thermal energy sources, significantly expanding the scope of renewable energy to seven types [52, 57, 62, 65, 77, 90, 91, 93, 97, 101, 102], with the potential to supply heating to 3 million households [77]. Regional achievements are also prominent, with Inje County being recognized as a leading local government in renewable energy dissemination and receiving an award from the Minister of Climate [56, 58, 69, 70, 88, 94]. Furthermore, Daejeon City is actively fostering the solar power industry and hosting renewable energy policy forums [64, 73, 78, 85, 95], and international cooperation is also active, with KEPCO E&C jointly developing a 500MW offshore wind power project in Vietnam [82, 84]. However, challenges such as the instability of the renewable energy system, high reliance on Chinese-made components in the solar and wind power sectors [60, 89], and issues like grid expansion, delays, and cost increases in thermal energy projects are also being raised [63, 76, 98].

sections.title: 🌍 COP31 Opening and the Current State of International Climate Action
sections.content: With COP31 opening in Türkiye, discussions on the current state of international climate action are active [109, 131, 138]. The UNFCCC's '2026 Global Climate Action Yearbook' revealed implementation gaps in six key areas alongside tangible achievements [19], and the UN Secretary-General called efforts to curb global warming a 'moment of truth,' pointing out insufficient global climate action [122, 127, 145]. At COP31, various agendas are being addressed, including the argument that resilience must be prioritized as farmers grapple with Super El Niño [115], the necessity of a 'peace dividend' to address the environmental costs of war [116], and pressure to ensure the true cleanliness of electrification [121, 140]. Meanwhile, an analysis suggested that the Iran conflict contributed slightly to reducing fossil fuel carbon emissions [105, 144, 148], but experts emphasize the need for further acceleration of clean energy to reach peak global CO2 emissions and begin their decline [108].

briefing.closing: Today's briefing has addressed the reality of the climate crisis, while also highlighting the multifaceted domestic and international efforts and challenges to overcome it. This is a time that demands sustained attention and action. This concludes the climate briefing for November 10, 2026.
